 Things To Do Things to do in Bali when it rains: a local’s guide to wet season
 By Ericko Dimas • 17 Nov 2026 
 Copy link Share via Telegram Share via WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X (Twitter) Share on LinkedIn Share via Email Rain in Bali usually comes in hard and leaves fast, but when it settles in for the afternoon, you need a plan B. 
 Raise your hand if you hate rainy season (me too!). Being stuck indoors with nothing to do is the worst . Well, worry not, because I’ve cracked the code. It turns out there are plenty of things to do in Bali when it rains, most of which you’d happily do on a sunny day too. Here’s where I go when the sky opens, from Sanur’s IMAX screen to workshops in Seminyak.
 FYI: Bali’s wet season runs from November to March, with January being the wettest month. Most downpours last a few hours rather than the whole day, so treat these as a half-day fix until the sun comes back. Still planning your dates? Our monthly Bali weather guide breaks it down.
 Why trust this guide
 Hi, I’m Erick, and as I’m writing this, it’ll be my second rainy season in Bali. I live in Sanur, and rainy season means I’ve had to master the art of planning my weekends around a downpour. Most of the spots in this guide are places I’ve been to myself, and the rest come from our team’s own visits and reviews (we use our own pics too!). Prices and opening hours were checked in November 2026, but they change often, so it’s worth confirming with the venue before you go.

 Bali rainy season starter pack 
 Before you head out, here’s what I’d keep on hand in wet season:
 A poncho, not an umbrella. Bali rain loves to come in sideways, and an umbrella won’t stand a chance. All the minimarts sell cheap jas hujan (raincoats) for emergencies, but it’s best to bring a good-quality one.
 Sandals you don’t mind soaking. Leave the white sneakers at the villa. Low-lying streets in Kuta and Seminyak can flood fast after a heavy downpour.
 Mosquito repellent. Mosquitoes love wet season, and dengue cases tend to rise with the rain, so spray up before you go out.
 A dry bag or waterproof phone pouch. It’s a lifesaver if you’re hopping on the back of a bike when the sky suddenly goes black.
 The MyBluebird app on your phone. Grab and Gojek aren’t reliable in rainy season (yes, even if you book a car). But Bluebird taxis seem to always show up, rain or shine.
 A light jacket for areas like Ubud or Kintamani. Rainy season up in the hills is the closest Bali gets to jumper weather, especially in the evenings.
 The Info BMKG app. Indonesia’s official weather agency posts local forecasts, which helps you plan around the worst of it.
 Where to go in Bali when it rains 
 1. Book a staycation at one of Bali’s best hotels 
 COMO Shambhala Estate is a five-star wellness retreat with its very own natural healing springs. (Photo by Honeycombers) When the forecast says rain all weekend, lean into it. Check into a resort with enough going on inside the gates that you never need to call a Grab, then spend the downpour shuffling between the spa and the restaurant.
 Here’s an unpopular opinion: rainy season is a blessing for staycation lovers, because that’s when the deals happen. Wet season is low season in Bali (Christmas and New Year aside), so luxury hotels and villas roll out some great rates. I round them up every month in our Bali hotel deals guide . Once you’ve booked, why not max it out? Here are my faves:
 AYANA Resort Bali – Jimbaran
 AYANA Resort Bali ‘s 90-hectare clifftop estate above Jimbaran Bay is practically a small town, with 19 restaurants and bars, a free shuttle between them and access to its sister hotel, RIMBA. On a wet day, book a treatment at the spa with its seawater hydrotherapy pool, then walk over to SAKA Museum, which is free for guests.
 Best for: Couples and families who want everything on site.
 Address: Jl. Karang Mas Sejahtera, Jimbaran 
 Price: From IDR 5,500,000++ per night
 COMO Shambhala Estate, Ubud 
 COMO Shambhala Estate is the pick for wellness enthusiasts. Here, days revolve around yoga, pilates and wellness classes, and there are three natural spring-fed pools if you’d rather float through a drizzle. The suites and villas are generously spread to give you peace and quiet. Each has its own terrace, oasis-like pool and even a yoga mat and meditation space.
 Best for: A luxury stay experience, riverside location, and nature-led wellness with expert guidance.
 Address: Banjar Begawan, Desa Melinggih, Ubud .
 Price: Starting from IDR 19,800,000 per night
 Capella Ubud, Keliki
 There’s something about rain drumming on canvas, and Capella Ubud has 22 of Bill Bensley’s tented villas in the rainforest north of Ubud, each with its own saltwater pool. The theme is a camp of 1800s explorers, so every tent has a different character, from the Cartographer to the Puppet Master. Book it when you want to romanticise the rain, and rainy season in Ubud is basically the closest thing Bali has to sweater weather!
 Best for: Couples looking to spend rainy season glamping in luxury tents in Ubud.
 Address: Jl Raya Dalem, Banjar Triwangsa, Desa Keliki, Tegallalang, Ubud 
 Price: From IDR 18,000,000 per night
 For more ideas, check out our full guide to the best luxury hotels and resorts in Bali! 
 2. Get busy with a Bali workshop 
 Making my signature scent at Umah Living, with 90 minutes of blending, tweaking and testing. (Photo by Honeycombers) Rainy days are made for learning something with your hands, and Bali’s craft scene runs deep. You’ll leave with a souvenir you made yourself, which beats another sarong from the market. Most studios work on bookings, so message them a day or two ahead. Here are some workshops I’ve tried myself and loved. In fact, I still keep my creations to this day:
 Candle and Room Spray Workshop at Umah Living – Seminyak
 Umah Living is a Bali-born fragrance house, and their 90-minute workshop lets you blend your own candle and room spray from around 80 fragrance oils. Founder Dino Lim guided my session, and the fun part is testing blends as many times as you like until it smells right. You go home with a soy and coconut wax candle, a room spray and a written recipe to recreate your scent later. You can read my full review of the Umah Living workshop .
 Best for: Anyone who wants a personalised scent souvenir to take home.
 Address: Jl. Mertanadi No.72, Kerobokan 
 Price: IDR 550,000 per person
 Paint a Pot at Jenggala – Jimbaran
 Jenggala has been making ceramics in Bali since the 1970s, and their Jimbaran flagship lets you pick a piece and paint it however you like. Kids love it, and so do adults who can’t commit to a full wheel class. Your piece gets fired in the on-site kilns and is ready to collect in five to seven days, so it’s best if you’re staying longer.
 Best for: Families on longer stays looking for an indoor crafty activity.
 Address: Jl. Uluwatu II, Jimbaran 
 Price: From IDR 150,000 per piece
 Jewellery Master Class at John Hardy – Mambal
 For a splurge, John Hardy’s bamboo workshop in Mambal runs a four-hour master class with their artisans, where you can learn traditional techniques or customise your own piece. It takes place during weekdays from 10am to 2pm and needs booking two days ahead. Read more about the John Hardy Jewellery Master Class .
 Best for: Jewellery lovers ready to splurge on a one-of-a-kind keepsake.
 Address: John Hardy Kapal Bamboo Boutique and Workshop, Mambal, Abiansemal 
 Price: From IDR 4,000,000 nett per person, including an IDR 2,000,000 gift card to spend at the boutique on the day.
 3. Visit an indoor adventure park 
 Geared up and ready to dive into the neon adventure at AeroXSpace! (Photo by Honeycombers) Got kids bouncing off the villa walls? Bali now has a few big indoor parks with air con, a roof and enough rides to burn off a whole afternoon of energy. All three below are located around Sanur and Denpasar, so factor in the drive if you’re coming from Canggu or Uluwatu.
 AeroXSpace – Sanur
 Here’s a fun indoor playground for everyone. Let me introduce you to  AeroXSpace . It’s Bali’s largest indoor adventure park with around 26 attractions and 3,500 square metres of air-conditioned space. Older kids can tackle the climbing walls, rope course and Supernova Slides, then ride the 100-metre Space Coaster. There’s a Toddler Space for under-sevens, and kids aged eight and up can play without an adult. On Saturday nights, the Galaxy Glow Party turns the lights down and the neon up from 5pm to 9pm.
 Best for: Active kids aged eight and up who need to burn off energy on a wet day in Bali.
 Address: Jl. Bypass Ngurah Rai No.999, Sidakarya, Sanur 
 Price:  IDR 175,000 for international visitors, IDR 150,000 for KTP and KITAS holders.
 Clip ‘n Climb Bali – Sanur
 Another win for Sanurians (like me!), Clip ‘n Climb is a local favourite for an indoor activity. It’s a climbing centre with 25 colourful challenges reaching up to nine metres, plus an augmented reality bouldering wall with more than 10 games. It’s open to anyone aged four and up, so it works for mixed-age families.
 Best for: Mixed-age families with little climbers aged four and up.
 Address: Jl. Bypass Ngurah Rai, Sanur Kauh, Denpasar 
 Price: Starting from IDR 220,000 for international visitors, IDR 150,000 for KTP and KITAS holders.
 Trans Studio Bali – Denpasar
 Trans Studio Bali takes up the top floor of Trans Studio Mall on Jalan Imam Bonjol, split into five themed zones. Expect a zombie-fighting simulator, Flying Over Indonesia (a virtual ride across the archipelago) and indoor skydiving, which costs extra. The rooftop coaster sits outside, so it may pause when the rain gets heavy, but there’s plenty more to do inside.
 Best for: Teens and thrill seekers who want a full day of rides under one roof.
 Address: Trans Studio Mall, Jl. Imam Bonjol No.440, Denpasar 
 Price: Around IDR 600,000 for international visitors, with cheaper rates for KITAS and KTP holders.
 Need more ideas? Check out our guide to all the best things to do with kids in Bali .  
 4. Relax at a spa 
 Spring Spa is a celeb-fave chain treating Uluwatu’s spa crew to some of the chicest treatments around. (Photo by Honeycombers) There’s no better soundtrack for a massage than rain on the roof. Bali has spas for every budget and every neighbourhood, so you can usually find one close enough to reach before the roads flood (yes, it happens sometimes). Here are a few favourites:
 Bodyworks Spa – Seminyak
 Even after two decades, Bodyworks Spa in Seminyak still deserves a top spot on your Bali spa bucket list. This iconic spa is renowned for its highly trained therapists and Moroccan palace-like interiors, and it really is as gorgeous as the photos. Here, you’ll find all the authentic Indonesian spa treatments you’d expect: deeply relaxing Balinese massages, nourishing cream baths, and mandi lulur – an ancient Javanese beauty ritual (and Indonesia’s secret to glowing skin).
 Recommended treatments: Mandi Lulur, Balinese Massage
 Address:   Jl Lebak Sari No. 3, Petitenget, Seminyak 
 Price: a 70-minute massage starts from IDR 650,000++
 Spring Spa – Uluwatu
 There are Spring Spa locations all over Bali, but the Uluwatu address is my favourite. Maybe it’s the architecturally perfected minimalist decor that had me falling head over heels for this spa sanctuary. This spa brand is actually from New Zealand, and it’s a bit of a celebrity favourite. Book a massage, then add the Twinkle Toes pedicure while you wait for the rain to clear.
 Recommended treatments: Twinkle Toes, Active Recovery Massage
 Address:   Jl Raya Labuansait No. 10, Uluwatu 
 Price: a 60-minute massage starts from IDR 310,000++
 Taksu Spa – Ubud
 Taksu Spa sits on Jalan Goutama, the same lane as Paradiso, so you can pair a premium Balinese massage with a film and dinner without getting back in the car. Their combined 90 years of experience in Indonesia’s wellness industry and healing rituals make them the best of the best not only in Ubud, but across Bali. You’ll find a full range of body treatments, from massages and reflexology to body scrubs, wraps and masks. They even offer multi-treatment spa packages and the revered ozone therapy.
 Recommended treatments: Premium Balinese Massage, Ingham Reflexology 
Address:  Jl Goutama Selatan, Ubud 
 Price: a 60-minute massage starts from IDR 450,000++
 Bali has way more spas than I can count, and you’ll probably find one every few metres. We’ve listed our top picks in our Best Spas & Massages in Bali guide. 
 5. Join a yoga class 
 Yoga is what I reach for whenever I need a break from the laptop. (Photo by Honeycombers) A 90-minute flow under a shala roof while the rain hammers down outside is peak Bali. Most drop-in classes cost between IDR 120,000 and IDR 185,000, and you don’t need to book a retreat to join. Just check the schedule and turn up early.
 Trending Now Add to calendar: Annual events you can't miss! 
 The Yoga Barn – Ubud
 The Yoga Barn is Ubud’s best-known yoga centre, running classes across several shalas from morning to evening, covering everything from vinyasa to sound healing. Daily classes are drop-in only and first come, first served, with registration opening at reception 30 minutes before each class. As one of the largest yoga centres in Southeast Asia, they also have guest houses, Garden Kafe, cacao and juice bars, and if you’re really ready for a big life change, you can even enrol onto yoga teacher training courses.
 Address: Jl. Hanoman, Pengosekan, Ubud 
 Price: From IDR 165,000++ per drop-in class
 Radiantly Alive – Ubud
 Radiantly Alive is right in central Ubud on Jalan Jembawan, so it’s easy to reach on foot when the traffic grinds to a halt in the rain. Beyond their signature vinyasa and Kundalini classes, they also offer workshops for sound healing, mindfulness and trauma release – the options for radiating from the inside out are endless.
 Address: Jl. Jembawan No.3, Ubud 
 Price: IDR 165,000 per drop-in class
 Samadi Bali, Canggu
 This Echo Beach studio is known for aerial yoga, inversions and kirtan sessions, and there’s an organic cafe on site for a post-class smoothie while you wait out the weather. Samadi Bali also brings in the best yoga teachers in Bali who have trained extensively across the island and around the world.
 Address: Jl. Padang Linjong No.39, Echo Beach, Canggu 
 Price: IDR 155,000 per drop-in class
 For more studios, see our guide to the best yoga studios in Bali . 
 6. Catch a film at Bali’s cinemas 
 Blanket on and seat fully reclined, the best way to sit out a downpour. (Photo by Honeycombers) If there’s one thing Indonesia does better than most, it’s cinemas. Picture a fully reclining seat with a blanket and food brought straight to you, all for around IDR 150,000 (about USD 8). And that’s the fanciest class. Regular seats cost half that (even less at the smaller malls in Denpasar). Hollywood films screen in English with Indonesian subtitles, and many Indonesian films come with English subtitles, so don’t worry about not understanding a thing. Oh, and the best part? You don’t have to queue anymore. Download TIX ID and you can book tickets for both XXI and Cinepolis in one app, premium seats included. Here are the cinemas I keep going back to:
 ICON Bali XXI – Sanur 
 ICON Bali is home to the island’s first IMAX with Laser screen, so this is where to watch anything big and loud. The IMAX hall seats 264, and there’s a 40-seat Premiere studio if you’d rather get comfy in the fully reclining seat with a blanket on and food brought to your seat.
 Address: Jl. Danau Tamblingan No.27, Sanur 
 Price: IMAX 3D from IDR 50,000 and Premiere from IDR 100,000
 Cinepolis Lippo Mall – Kuta 
 The main reason I go here is for the price. Regular screens can go for as low as IDR 25,000 (around USD 1.5) and you can get in-seat dining for the price of a decent lunch. They also have a VIP class with the same facilities you get at XXI Premiere.
 Address: Jl. Kartika Plaza No.15 Lt. LG, Kuta 
 Price: Regular screen from IDR 25,000 and VIP from IDR 75,000
 Paradiso – Ubud 
 Paradiso is the anti-multiplex. Rather than just the latest blockbusters, Ubud’s indie cinema mixes classics and documentaries with the odd recent release. The schedule changes daily and goes up on Paradiso’s Instagram .
 Address: Jl. Goutama Sel., Ubud 
 Price: From IDR 75,000 (including an IDR 50,000 F&B credit)
 7. Go museum hopping 
 Museum Pasifika isn’t just an art museum – they host art classes and workshops too! A wet afternoon is the best excuse to finally do the museums you keep saying you’ll get to. Ubud has the biggest cluster, while the south has two highlights in Nusa Dua and Jimbaran. A heads-up for the older Ubud museums, though. Galleries are often split across garden pavilions, so pack an umbrella for the dash between buildings. Some inspo on which museums to visit during your holiday:
 SAKA Museum – Jimbaran
 SAKA Museum is part of AYANA Bali and is built around Nyepi and the Balinese Saka calendar. It also made TIME’s World’s Greatest Places list in 2024. The showstopper is the hall of towering ogoh-ogoh , the demon effigies paraded the night before the Day of Silence (learn more about Nyepi in Bali). There’s also a gallery on subak , Bali’s centuries-old rice irrigation system, and a cafe for when you’re done.
 Best for: Anyone curious about Nyepi and the cultural background behind ogoh-ogoh. 
 Address: AYANA Estate, Jl. Karang Mas Sejahtera, Jimbaran 
 Price: Free for AYANA guests, general admission from around IDR 300,000
 Museum Puri Lukisan – Ubud
 Open since 1956, Puri Lukisan is Ubud’s oldest art museum and the best crash course in traditional Balinese painting and woodcarving. It’s a short walk from Ubud Palace on Jalan Raya Ubud, so you can duck in when the rain starts mid-wander.
 Best for: Art lovers wanting a crash course in traditional Balinese painting and woodcarving. 
Address:   Jl. Raya Ubud, Ubud 
 Price: IDR 95,000 (kids under 15 get in free)
 Museum Pasifika – Nusa Dua
 More than 600 artworks by over 200 artists from 25 countries fill the halls at Museum Pasifika , with names like Adrien-Jean Le Mayeur, Theo Meier and Affandi. It’s inside the ITDC complex in Nusa Dua, which makes it an easy add-on if you’re staying at one of the big resorts. Read our full guide to Museum Pasifika if you’re curious to find out more.
 Best for:  Nusa Dua resort guests who want a museum within walking distance.
 Address: ITDC Bali Tourism Complex, Block P, Nusa Dua 
 Price: IDR 100,000 for international visitors and IDR 70,000 for KTP holders.
 8. Go shopping at Bali’s best malls 
 The floating market at ICON Bali is my favourite place to people-watch while the rain passes. (Photo by Honeycombers) Having grown up in Jakarta (AKA Indonesia’s city of malls), I’ll be honest. Bali’s malls won’t win any prizes for originality, except maybe the beachfront ones like Beachwalk and ICON Bali. However, on a grey day, a few hours of air con, shopping and a decent lunch can save the afternoon. Most open from around 10am to 10pm, and the bigger ones double up as entertainment hubs with cinemas and arcades. I can easily spend a whole day at these malls:
 ICON Bali – Sanur
 I’m biased because this one is closest to my apartment. I may or may not have picked my apartment based on this mall (but that’s another story). This is one of the island’s biggest malls, with around 200 tenants. Expect all the popular stores like Uniqlo, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Krisna for oleh-oleh , plus a floating market of local stalls selling traditional Indonesian snacks like klepon , es cendol and risol .
 Address: Jl. Danau Tamblingan No.27, Sanur 
 Seminyak Village – Seminyak
 Smaller and calmer than the big Denpasar malls, Seminyak Village is where to go for local designer labels and gallery browsing without leaving Seminyak. It’s a solid stop if you’re staying nearby and don’t fancy a long drive in the rain.
 Address: Jl. Kayu Jati No.8, Seminyak 
 Beachwalk Shopping Center – Kuta
 Beachwalk sits right across the road from Kuta Beach, with a mix of international brands and local boutiques, plus restaurants facing the ocean. It’s partly open-air, so it’s better for a drizzle than a full-on storm, but the shops and the Cinema XXI Premiere upstairs keep you dry. If the rain stops by late afternoon, grab a table facing the beach for sunset. There’s also a free seating area called the Sunset Deck, where I’ve spent countless afternoons.
 Address: Jl. Pantai Kuta, Kuta 
 More things to do in Bali when it rains 
 Take a Balinese cooking class
 Cooking classes happen under a roof, last half a day and end with a long lunch, which makes them a no-brainer when the weather turns. In Ubud, Casa Luna Cooking School runs a different themed class almost every day, while Paon Bali teaches you in a family kitchen in Laplapan village for around IDR 350,000. Some include a morning market tour, so pick an afternoon class if the forecast looks grim. Browse more options in our guide to the best cooking classes in Bali .
 Watch the Devdan Show in Nusa Dua
 The Devdan Show is a one-hour, fully indoor production at the Bali Nusa Dua Theatre, mixing acrobatics, aerial dance and traditional performances from Bali, Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua. It’s a family-friendly alternative to the Kecak dance at Uluwatu, which is outdoors and at the mercy of the weather. Shows run on Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday at 7.30pm.
 Crack an escape room in Kuta
 Got a competitive group? Pandora Experience Escape Room in Kuta has seven themed games, from Alcatraz and Area 51 to the Tomb of Osiris, and gives teams of two to eight people two hours to get out. It’s a fun, slightly chaotic way to spend a stormy evening with friends.
 Rainy season gets a bad rap, but some of my favourite Bali days have started with a downpour and ended in a cinema recliner or a candle-making class. Book the popular spots a day ahead, and save the beach for when the sun comes back out (it usually doesn’t take long!). 
 Rainy day in Bali FAQs 
 What can you do in Bali when it rains? 
 Head indoors. Catch a film at ICON Bali XXI in Sanur or Paradiso in Ubud, visit SAKA Museum in Jimbaran or Museum Puri Lukisan in Ubud, or book a spa, yoga or cooking class. Families can spend the afternoon at Trans Studio Bali or AeroXSpace in Denpasar.
 When is rainy season in Bali? 
 Bali's wet season runs from November to March. January is usually the wettest month, and March is when the rain starts to ease off.
 Does it rain all day in Bali during wet season? 
 Rarely. Most downpours last from a few minutes to a few hours, often overnight or in the early morning, and the sun usually comes back out afterwards. That's why half-day plans like a film, a massage or a workshop work so well.
 Where can kids play indoors in Bali? 
 Trans Studio Bali on Jalan Imam Bonjol in Denpasar is the island's big indoor theme park. AeroXSpace and Clip 'n Climb Bali, both on the bypass near Sanur, are good for active kids.
 What can you do in Ubud when it rains? 
 Ubud has plenty. Visit Museum Puri Lukisan on Jalan Raya Ubud, watch a film at Paradiso on Jalan Goutama, book a silver class at Studio Perak or a cooking class at Casa Luna, or drop into a yoga class at The Yoga Barn or Radiantly Alive.
 What can you do in Canggu and Seminyak when it rains? 
 Book a massage at AMO Spa in Canggu or Bodyworks in Seminyak, take an aerial yoga class at Samadi Bali or a hot yoga class at Jiwa Bali, or browse the boutiques at Seminyak Village.
